headline: Sir Colin Birss, the judiciary's lead judge for AI, has set out a "cautious but positive" approach under which judges may use approved AI tools as long as they check and answer for every output.
score_reason: Pool 4 lowered by 1: the statement was issued 'last week', before the window, and the Gazette article could not be opened, so the story rests on Legal Futures.
importance_line: Anyone whose case is heard in court, and the lawyers and court staff around them, will meet AI tools that judges are now allowed to use, with the judge fully accountable for the result, but Legal Futures dates the statement only to last week.
summary: Legal Futures reports that Sir Colin Birss, the judge who leads the judiciary's work on AI and who becomes Master of the Rolls (a senior judge in England and Wales) next month, issued a position statement last week saying the judiciary will take a "cautious but positive" approach to AI, backed by pilots and strict safeguards. The statement says every AI output used in judicial work must be reviewed, verified and approved by the responsible judge, and that only approved tools may be used, with features including UK data residency, enterprise data protection and web access switched off.
notes: The pool link (The Law Society Gazette) returned HTTP 405 and could not be opened; the same story was read on Legal Futures and is credited to it, and url points to that page. The Gazette also carries the story. Legal Futures dates the statement only as 'last week', so freshness is NEW and the exact date is unconfirmed.
